extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral philosophy; historians of ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Critical historical and philosophical analysis of theories about conscience, motives, virtue, and utilitarianism from classical and modern writers. The page surveys competing definitions and standards for what makes actions virtuous or morally blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as 'opinion of evidence' (Hobbes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes defines conscience as 'the opinion of evidence' (On Human Nature, ch. vi. §8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one historical account of conscience emphasizing cognitive/judgmental aspect; included among other, often contrasting definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as self-judgment of moral rectitude (Locke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke defines conscience as 'our own opinion or judgment of the moral rectitude or pravity of our own actions' (Essay, book i. ch. iii. § 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames conscience as an internal evaluative faculty; compared with Hobbes, Bentham, Bain, and others to show divergent conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as fictitious seat in the mind / love of duty as love of power (Bentham)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bentham treats conscience as 'a thing of fictitious existence, supposed to occupy a seat in the mind' (Deontology) and ranks 'love of duty' as a variety of 'love of power' (Springs of Action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents the utilitarian/psychological-reductionist stance that conscience and duty are not sui generis moral principles but psychological phenomena reducible to other motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as imitation of external government (Bain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Bain: 'conscience is an imitation within ourselves of the government without us.' (Emotions and Will, p. 313.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the social/imitative origin of conscience; used to contrast ideas of innate moral law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue can become both instrument and part of happiness (Mill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill: though virtue may originally be desired as an instrument for happiness, it can 'come to be desired ... as part of happiness' — virtue is capable of becoming an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reconcile utilitarianism with moral motives that seem disinterested: practices originally useful can acquire intrinsic value through human psychology and habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive composition and competing motives model (Mill's example of adultery)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agent faced with temptation obeys the strongest motives; pleasures and pains associated with an act (including social reproach, injured parties' pain, self-reproach) compete, and habitual associations determine disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains moral action as the balance of associated pleasures and pains; education and habits shape which motives predominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct divine disinterestedness vs human imperfect imitation (Tucker / theological view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tucker: God's goodness is 'pure, disinterested bounty' beyond self-regarding increase; humans lack that pure disinterestedness and so have imperfect notions of such a quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between theological claim that true disinterested goodness exists only in deity and moralists (e.g., Hutcheson) who ask why some degree of similar public love might exist in humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habituation: actions become desired without reference to end (habit-formation account of virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Through association we 'come to desire the means without thinking of the end; the action itself becomes an object of desire, and is performed without reference to any motive beyond itself' (Mill, Logic). Habits can persist even when no longer pleasurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain how moral habits and heroism persist despite suffering or absent reward; also explains persistence of harmful habits once de-linked from pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness redefined as absence of self-regarding interests (Bentham/Tucker analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the only true sense disinterestedness denotes absence of all interest of the self-regarding class; but human actions are never free from interest — the label 'disinterested' often masks continued influence of other interests (hope/fear of God, reputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that 'disinterestedness' is typically a language/terminology issue rather than proof of actuating absence of interest; caution against sloppy use of the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: All motives as pursuit of pleasure/avoidance of pain (Bentham)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bentham: 'Pleasure is itself a good ... Pain is in itself an evil ... No man has ever had, can, or could have a motive different from the pursuit of pleasure or of shunning pain.' (Principles of Morals and Legislation; Deontology)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thoroughgoing psychological utilitarian claim that reduces moral psychology to hedonic calculation; Mill modifies by distinguishing moral worth of agent from rightness of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive's role in morality vs moral estimation of agent (Mill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill: 'The motive has nothing to do with the morality of the action, though much with the worth of the agent' — motives don't change whether an act is right, but affect our estimate of the actor's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to separate concept of right action (consequentialist criterion) from praise/blame (character evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of universalizability test for consequences (Lecky/Austin critique of utilitarian sophistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to judge remote consequences of an action by asking 'if acts of this class were generally done ... what would be the probable effect' — the correct inquiry is how far the act is likely to produce imitators or affect future conduct; classifications of general tendency cannot alter morality of particular acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky warns against simplistically applying a 'if everyone did it' test; emphasises factual assessment of causal effects and imitation probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarian measurement of virtue by balance of good over harm (Comte / Benthamian calculus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue's greatness is evaluated by comparing the goods obtained with the evils paid for them: 'the excess in good measures the value of virtue, as the excess in evil measures the degree of hate due to vice.' (Ch. Comte)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses the quantitative/comparative approach to moral valuation prevalent in utilitarian and consequentialist thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vengeance and punishment as utilitarian pleasures (Dumont/Bentham on vengeance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of vengeance (satisfaction causing pain to the delinquent) is treated as a gain; vengeance may be cultivated as a legitimate pleasure if it yields net benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates utilitarian willingness to count otherwise morally charged feelings (revenge) within the hedonic calculus; raises moral tensions with common-sense condemnations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education directs dispositions (Adam Smith on directing vanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam Smith: 'the great secret of education is to direct vanity to proper objects.' (Moral Sentiments) — education shapes which motives and vanities guide behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion: moral formation depends on directing natural motives toward socially beneficial ends; used to explain variation in dispositions across people/classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral feelings and self-approbation vs religious humility distinction (Smith/Butler debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smith depicts self-approval arising from virtuous action as pleasure distinct from religious sense of humility or divine favour; Butler suggests a perfect man would be the last to know it — humility differs from utilitarian self-gratulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against conflating secular self-satisfaction with religious humility; useful when assessing motives behind virtuous acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity of sensibility increases pains as well as moral progress (Tucker/Hartley observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick sensibility that advances perfection also heightens pungency of pains and vexations; intense compassion can sometimes divert from charity (Butler) by making one turn away from the miserable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights trade-off: moral refinement brings both greater capacity for good and increased exposure to suffering; relevant for evaluating consequences of cultivating sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social penalties for conscientious minority behavior (Lecky/Social consequence of conscience)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tradesman resisting dishonest custom or a soldier refusing duels may incur full social penalties for failing to follow illegal or common practices; conscience-driven acts can be socially costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when assessing real-world consequences of moral actions that conflict with prevailing laws/customs; indicates conscience may require sacrifice and attract punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual virtue persists beyond expedience (Tucker/other exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues, once habituated, continue to operate 'after their expedience ceases' and may persist even where they yield no further advantage; moral heroes persevere despite suffering because of this habit-formed will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains endurance of virtue independent of immediate pleasure — important for accounting for actions that produce pain yet are still judged virtuous.
